The `probarion` CLI dry-runs a spend, checks a payee, verifies a vault, exports the ledger, generates keys and prints the transactions that a vault's owner and approvers sign. It signs nothing itself: for each owner or approver call it checks your input against the contract's rules, writes the arguments to a file and prints the near-cli-rs command for that person to sign. The tables below list every command and option of the CLI, version 0.1.1, as `packages/cli/src/program.ts` builds it in this repository, and a test fails when the code gains or loses a command or an option that they do not list. `payee check` is in this repository and newer than 0.1.1, the release on npm, so `npx probarion` does not have it yet: run it in a clone, as `node packages/cli/dist/bin.js payee check ...`.

## How to read the tables

Each table holds one command group, and each row one command. A row's anchor is its command with `cli-` in front and hyphens for spaces: `vault create` is at [`#cli-vault-create`](#cli-vault-create).

- **Command** is what follows the program name. Only `help` and `payee check` take a positional argument: `help` takes the command whose help it prints, and `payee check` the payee it checks. Every other input is an option. In your own project folder, run a command as `npx probarion vault create ...`, or as `probarion vault create ...` after `npm install -g probarion`. In a clone of the repository, run the CLI the clone builds, as `node packages/cli/dist/bin.js vault create ...`. [Install the packages](/docs/build/install) has both.
- **Options** lists every option of the command, spelled as the CLI's help spells it. "(required)" means the command stops with an error without that option. "(default `x`)" is the value the option takes when you leave it out. Every command but `help` also takes `--help`.
- **Who signs** names the account whose wallet signs the printed near-cli-rs command, with the prepaid gas and the deposit that command attaches. "Nothing" means the command prints no transaction.

The placeholders in the options mean:

- `<usdc>`: an amount in USDC with up to 6 decimals, so `--amount 25` is 25 USDC.
- `<near>`: an amount in NEAR with up to 24 decimals.
- `<id>`: after `--vault`, a NEAR account id. After `--mandate` or `--spend`, a whole number: ids start at 1.
- `<pk>`: an ed25519 public key, written `ed25519:...`.
- `<account>`: a NEAR account id. `<list>`: account ids separated by commas.

Three options recur. `--vault <id>` falls back to `PROBARION_VAULT_ID`, and every command that has the option needs one of the two, except `payee check`, which warns without one, and `verify --offline`, which refuses it. `--sign-as <account>` writes the signer into the printed command. Without it, the command holds a placeholder such as `<owner-account-id>`, which the shell refuses as pasted. `--out-dir <dir>` is the folder for the arguments file. [Configure](/docs/build/install#configure) lists every environment variable the CLI reads.

## Program options

These options belong to the program, not to one command, so each appears here and in no command row. They can come before the command words, as in `npx probarion --network testnet vault freeze --vault <vault>`, or after them. NEAR testnet is live today. On mainnet one small vault runs, `v0.probarion.near`, and no mainnet factory is deployed: see [Testnet and mainnet](/docs/start/testnet-and-mainnet).

<RefTable id="cli-program-options" />

## What a signing command prints

<Callout kind="owner-signs">

The command in this section prints a call for the owner to sign. Review the arguments file and its sha256 first, then sign with your own wallet, keychain or Ledger.

</Callout>

Run in your own project folder, this command prints the `revoke_mandate` call for mandate 1 of an illustrative testnet vault. It reads nothing from the chain, and it writes the arguments file into the folder:

```bash
npx probarion --network testnet mandate revoke --vault acme.vaults.probarion.testnet --mandate 1
```

```text
OWNER SIGNS: probarion never signs owner or approver transactions. Review the arguments, then sign with your own wallet or near-cli-rs:

near contract call-function as-transaction acme.vaults.probarion.testnet revoke_mandate file-args ./revoke_mandate.0a38f6055d2b.args.json prepaid-gas '30.0 Tgas' attached-deposit '1 yoctoNEAR' sign-as <owner-account-id> network-config testnet sign-with-keychain send
sha256 of the args file: 0a38f6055d2b1a7cf20555fde86bb075f5aee4957da14266e1982f4ed8200069  (check: sha256sum ./revoke_mandate.0a38f6055d2b.args.json, or Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 ./revoke_mandate.0a38f6055d2b.args.json in PowerShell)
Run it in bash, zsh or PowerShell (not cmd.exe).

revoke_mandate arguments (./revoke_mandate.0a38f6055d2b.args.json):
{
  "mandate_id": 1
}

Pending spends keep their reservation until they settle or fail; approve then refuses with MandateInactive.

With a Ledger hardware wallet, replace `sign-with-keychain send` with `sign-with-ledger usb send`.
```

Every command that prints a call prints these parts:

- **Who signs.** The first line starts with `OWNER SIGNS` or, for `spend approve` and `spend reject`, `APPROVER SIGNS`.
- **The arguments file**, named `<method>.<the first 12 hex of its sha256>.args.json`. The name follows the content, so a command you printed earlier keeps pointing at the arguments you reviewed. The CLI refuses to print over a file of that name whose content differs.
- **The sha256 of that file**, to check before you sign, with `sha256sum` or, in PowerShell, `Get-FileHash`.
- **The near-cli-rs command.** It ends with `sign-with-keychain send`, and runs in bash, zsh or PowerShell, not in cmd.exe.
- **A note** on what the call does once signed, from the same rules as the table's "What it does".

Before it prints, the CLI checks your input against the contract's rules. An input it refuses stops it with `error:` on stderr and exit code 1, and it writes no file.

## Vault commands

<Callout kind="owner-signs">

Every vault command prints a call the owner signs. [Vaults, roles and keys](/docs/concepts/vaults-roles-and-keys) explains the owner's role.

</Callout>

<RefTable id="cli-commands-vault" />

## Mandate commands

<Callout kind="owner-signs">

Both mandate commands print a call the owner signs. A mandate has no edit call: to change one, revoke it and create a new one. [Mandates](/docs/concepts/mandates) explains each limit.

</Callout>

<RefTable id="cli-commands-mandate" />

## Agent commands

<Callout kind="owner-signs">

`agent add` and `agent remove` print a call the owner signs. [Vaults, roles and keys](/docs/concepts/vaults-roles-and-keys) explains the agent key.

</Callout>

<RefTable id="cli-commands-agent" />

## Ledger commands

<Callout kind="owner-signs">

`ledger set-key` prints a call the owner signs. [The ledger and anchors](/docs/concepts/ledger-and-anchors) explains what the ledger key signs.

</Callout>

<RefTable id="cli-commands-ledger" />

## Spend commands

<Callout kind="approver-signs">

`spend approve` and `spend reject` print a call for an account in the vault's approver list to sign. The list decides, not the owner role: the owner can approve only when the list names it. One approver's call is enough. [Find the held spend](/docs/concepts/holds-and-approvals#find-the-held-spend) shows how to get the id that `--spend` takes.

</Callout>

<RefTable id="cli-commands-spend" />

## The check command

`check` is the dry run of a spend: it asks the vault whether its own spend checks would pass. [How a payment is checked](/docs/concepts/payment-checks) lists the checks, and [Errors](/docs/build/errors) explains each `PROBARION:<Code>` it can print.

<RefTable id="cli-commands-check" />

## Payee commands

`payee check` is advice for the owner before a mandate names a payee: it reads the chain, signs nothing and changes nothing on chain. A read it could not make warns, so the verdict is never `ALLOW`. It is in this repository and newer than npm 0.1.1. [Mandates](/docs/concepts/mandates#why-a-mandate-cannot-be-edited) explains why a mandate's payee never changes.

<RefTable id="cli-commands-payee" />

## The verify command

`verify` runs the verifier's nine checks against the chain, or against a saved snapshot. [Verifier checks a to i](/docs/trust/verifier-checks) says what each check proves, and [Verify a vault yourself](/docs/trust/verify-a-vault) walks through a run on a live vault.

<RefTable id="cli-commands-verify" />

## The help command

Commander, the CLI's argument parser, adds `help` to the program and to each command group on its own: no file in `packages/cli/src/commands` defines it.

<RefTable id="cli-commands-help" />

## Exit codes

`check`, `payee check` and `verify` give their result as the exit code, so a usage error of theirs exits 64 rather than 1, and a script can tell a refusal, a blocked payee or a failed check from a mistyped flag.

<RefTable id="cli-exit-codes" />

## What the tables do not cover

- **The calls themselves.** The contract methods behind each printed call, with their arguments and the checks they run, are on [Contract reference](/docs/build/contract-reference). The vault's own limits, such as its 10 approvers and 16 agent keys, are on [Limits and costs](/docs/build/limits-and-costs).
- **The meaning of a result.** A refusal code is on [Errors](/docs/build/errors), and a verifier row on [Verifier checks a to i](/docs/trust/verifier-checks).
- **The CLI as a library.** The `probarion` package also exports `runCli` and `buildProgram`, which this page does not document. Code that pays from an agent uses the SDK: see [SDK reference](/docs/build/sdk-reference).
- **Signing.** The CLI never runs near-cli-rs. You sign with your own wallet, and nothing the CLI prints is sent until you run it.
